statement: If from a medial straight line there be subtracted a medial straight line which is commensurable with the whole in square only, and which contains with the whole a rational rectangle, the remainder is irrational. And let it be called a first apotome of a medial straight line.
heath_proof: For from the medial straight line AB let there be subtracted the medial straight line BC which is commensurable with AB in square only and with AB makes the rectangle AB, BC rational; I say that the remainder AC is irrational; and let it be called a first apotome of a medial straight line. For, since AB, BC are medial, the squares on AB, BC are also medial. But twice the rectangle AB, BC is rational; therefore the squares on AB, BC are incommensurable with twice the rectangle AB, BC; therefore twice the rectangle AB, BC is also incommensurable with the remainder, the square on AC, [Cf. II. 7] since, if the whole is incommensurable with one of the magnitudes, the original magnitudes will also be incommensurable. [X. 16] But twice the rectangle AB, BC is rational; therefore the square on AC is irrational; therefore AC is irrational. [X. Def. 4] And let it be called a first apotome of a medial straight line.

10.74
**Statement:** If from a medial straight line there be subtracted a medial straight line which is commensurable with the whole in square only, and which contains with the whole a rational rectangle, the remainder is irrational. And let it be called a first apotome of a medial straight line.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a medial straight line, and from AB let there be subtracted the straight line BC, so that C lies on AB between A and B, where BC is medial, BC is commensurable with AB in square only, and the rectangle contained by AB, BC is rational. I say that the remainder AC is irrational.

**Step 2.** Since AB is medial, the square on AB is equal to a rectangle contained by two rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and such an area is irrational [10.21]; this area is what is called a medial area. Thus the square on AB is a medial area, and it is irrational, that is, incommensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out [D10.1.4]. In the same way the square on BC is a medial area.

**Step 3.** Since AB, BC are commensurable in square, the squares on AB, BC are measured by the same area, that is, they are commensurable with one another [D10.1.2]. Therefore, the two commensurable magnitudes, the square on AB and the square on BC, being added together, the whole, namely the sum of the squares on AB, BC, is commensurable with the square on AB [10.15].

**Step 4.** But the square on AB is a medial area (Step 2); and an area commensurable with a medial area is itself medial [10.23]. Therefore the sum of the squares on AB, BC is a medial area, and hence it is irrational [10.21], that is, incommensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out [D10.1.4].

**Step 5.** The rectangle AB, BC is rational by hypothesis, that is, it is commensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out [D10.1.4]. Now the rectangle AB, BC measures twice the rectangle AB, BC, so that the rectangle AB, BC and twice the rectangle AB, BC are measured by the same measure and are commensurable [D10.1.1]. Since twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the rectangle AB, BC, and the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out, twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with that square [10.12]; therefore twice the rectangle AB, BC is rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 6.** Since the straight line AB is cut at C, the square on the whole AB together with the square on the segment BC is equal to twice the rectangle contained by AB, BC together with the square on the remaining segment AC [2.7]. Thus the sum of the squares on AB, BC is a whole made up of two parts, namely twice the rectangle AB, BC and the square on AC.

**Step 7.** I say that the sum of the squares on AB, BC is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AB, BC. For, if it were commensurable with it, then, since twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out (Step 5), the sum of the squares on AB, BC would also be commensurable with that square [10.12], and so would be rational [D10.1.4]; but it is medial and irrational (Step 4), which is impossible. Therefore the sum of the squares on AB, BC is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AB, BC.

**Step 8.** Now the whole, the sum of the squares on AB, BC, is made up of twice the rectangle AB, BC and the square on AC (Step 6), and the whole is incommensurable with one of them, twice the rectangle AB, BC (Step 7). But if the whole be incommensurable with one of the magnitudes added together, the original magnitudes are incommensurable [10.16]. Therefore twice the rectangle AB, BC is incommensurable with the square on AC.

**Step 9.** I say that the square on AC is incommensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out. For, if it were commensurable with it, then, since twice the rectangle AB, BC is also commensurable with that square (Step 5), the square on AC would be commensurable with twice the rectangle AB, BC [10.12], contrary to Step 8. Therefore the square on AC is incommensurable with the square on the rational straight line set out, and so the square on AC is irrational [D10.1.4].

**Step 10.** Since the square on AC is an irrational area, the straight line AC, on which the square is described, is irrational [D10.1.4]. Therefore the remainder AC is irrational, which was to be proved. And let AC be called a first apotome of a medial straight line.
